lesson.title: From Counts to Proportions: Relative Frequency
lesson.summary: Relative frequency converts a raw count into a proportion of the whole group by dividing each frequency by the total, which is what makes fair comparisons between groups of different sizes possible.
lesson.body:
A frequency tells you how many individuals fall into a category, but it does not by itself tell you how large that category is compared to the whole group. Nine students with brown eyes sounds like a lot until you learn whether the class had 20 students or 200. Relative frequency solves this problem by converting each frequency into a proportion of the total, calculated as the frequency of a category divided by the total number of individuals in the data set.

Relative frequency can be reported as a decimal proportion, such as 0.45, or as a percent, such as 45 percent, by multiplying the proportion by 100. Because relative frequencies describe a share of the whole, every relative frequency in a distribution must fall between 0 and 1, and the relative frequencies across all categories of a single variable must always add up to 1, or 100 percent, since every individual belongs to exactly one category.

Returning to the eye color data from the frequency table, 20 students total with brown 9, blue 6, green 3, and hazel 2, the relative frequencies are found by dividing each frequency by 20. Brown: 9 divided by 20 equals 0.45, or 45 percent. Blue: 6 divided by 20 equals 0.30, or 30 percent. Green: 3 divided by 20 equals 0.15, or 15 percent. Hazel: 2 divided by 20 equals 0.10, or 10 percent. Checking the total: 0.45 plus 0.30 plus 0.15 plus 0.10 equals 1.00, confirming the relative frequencies were calculated correctly.

The real value of relative frequency shows up when comparing groups of different sizes. If a second school of 500 students had 200 with brown eyes, the raw frequency, 200, is far larger than this class's 9, but the relative frequency, 200 divided by 500, equals 0.40, or 40 percent, which is actually a slightly smaller share than this class's 45 percent. Relative frequency puts every group on the same 0 to 1 scale, which is exactly what makes a fair comparison possible.

Relative frequency also sets up two of the most important graphing tools in this course. A pie chart displays relative frequencies directly, since each slice's size is based on the proportion of the whole that a category represents, and cumulative relative frequency, covered next, builds on this same idea by tracking running totals of these proportions as you move through ordered categories or values.

A frequency table is often extended into a single combined table that lists each category alongside both its frequency and its relative frequency, which is convenient because it lets a reader see the raw count and the proportion at once. Applying this to the sibling count data from earlier, ten students with 0 siblings for 2 students, 1 sibling for 5 students, 2 siblings for 2 students, and 3 siblings for 1 student, the relative frequencies are 2 divided by 10 equals 0.20, 5 divided by 10 equals 0.50, 2 divided by 10 equals 0.20, and 1 divided by 10 equals 0.10. These again sum to 1.00 exactly, showing that the same addition check works no matter how many categories or values a variable has.
